prompt: Why can one copy of a model's weights in GPU memory serve many users at once?

options.A: The weights are recomputed for each request from the training data, so nothing has to be shared
options.B: At inference the weights are only read, never written; each request's activations are its own
options.C: Users take turns: the GPU serves one request at a time, fast enough that nobody notices the queue
options.D: Each user gets a private copy of the weights, loaded from disk into GPU memory when the session opens

prompt: Who decides a token's query, and how does it get good at finding useful words?

options.A: A learned matrix W_Q times the token's vector; training adjusts W_Q when a better query would lower the loss
options.B: It is drawn at random for each request, and attention averages over enough heads that the noise cancels out
options.C: The tokenizer assigns each token ID a fixed query when the vocabulary is built, before training starts
options.D: Engineers write rules for what each word should look for, and training tunes how strongly each rule fires

prompt: Blend two values with a weighted average: 4 with share 75%, 8 with share 25%.
Why run several attention heads instead of one, at the same total width?

options.A: Heads run on different layers, so splitting into several heads is how depth is added to the model
options.B: More heads add parameters even at the same total width, so the model can store more facts in each attention layer
options.C: Each head has its own softmax, so each can focus sharply on its own target; one softmax would blur them into one average
options.D: Heads are redundant copies that each compute the full attention, so if one produces bad scores the others outvote it

prompt: Why can't an LLM reliably count the r's in “strawberry”?

options.A: The word was rare in its training data, so the model never learned how many r's it contains
options.B: It sees a few token IDs (str + aw + berry); the letters inside each piece never reach it
options.C: Softmax rounds small counts to zero, so the third r gets a share too small to register
options.D: It reads the word one letter at a time but only remembers the last few letters it has seen

prompt: A model writes a 100-token answer. Roughly how many times does the whole model run?

options.A: Once per sentence: the model plans a sentence, then writes out its tokens
options.B: Once per layer, so 32 times for a 32-layer model, with every token made in that sweep
options.C: About 100: one pass per new token, each with the last token appended
options.D: Once: a single forward pass produces the whole 100-token answer at the same time

prompt: Why does it help that similar words have nearby rows?

options.A: It lets the tokenizer merge words with nearby rows into one token, which keeps sequences short
options.B: Nearby rows can share storage, so a model with many synonyms needs fewer numbers in its table
options.C: Similar inputs give similar outputs, so what it learned about “river flooded” carries over to “stream flooded”
options.D: The model answers by finding the training sentence whose rows are nearest to the prompt, so close rows match well

prompt: What does a gradient tell training?

options.A: For each number, how the error would change if it moved a little, so training steps each one downhill
options.B: Which neuron fired the most on the last example, so training can strengthen that one neuron alone
options.C: How big a step to take on this example: the learning rate training should use for every number
options.D: The correct next token at each position, so training can copy it straight into the output table

prompt: The same paragraph costs more tokens in Hindi than in English. Why can't fine-tuning the model fix this?

options.A: Hindi needs more weights per token, and fine-tuning can only adjust weights, never add new ones
options.B: The tokenizer is built and frozen before the model trains; training never changes how text is split
options.C: Fine-tuning could fix it by teaching the model longer Hindi pieces, but it costs too much to be worth it
options.D: Providers bill per word rather than per token, so the extra Hindi tokens are not what you pay for

prompt: “The river bank flooded” and “The bank raised rates”. Compare the row looked up for “bank” in the two sentences.

options.A: The same row at first, but the model edits that row in place for the money sentence
options.B: Different rows: the tokenizer reads the sentence and picks the water or money ID for bank
options.C: Identical: the same ID reads the same row; context is mixed in later by attention
options.D: Different rows, because the two “bank”s sit at different positions in their sentences

prompt: How does “an LLM is a function, not a lookup table” explain hallucination?

options.A: It scores a plausible next token for any input; nothing checks that a source for the claim exists
options.B: It retrieves the closest stored document from its training data and sometimes retrieves the wrong one
options.C: It comes only from sampling randomness, so at temperature 0 a model can no longer make up a fact
options.D: The fact's token is missing from the vocabulary, so the model substitutes the most similar token it has

prompt: An embedding table has one row per vocabulary token. Vocabulary 100,000, width 4,096. How many learned numbers are in the table, in millions?
Why can't a token ID be fed to the model as a plain number?

options.A: IDs are reassigned on every request, so the same word would reach the model as a different number each time
options.B: The model only accepts numbers between 0 and 1, so IDs are divided by the vocabulary size first
options.C: IDs run into the hundreds of thousands, too large for a GPU to multiply without overflowing its 16-bit numbers
options.D: IDs are labels, not quantities: 500 isn't “close to” 501 in meaning. Each ID selects a learned row instead

prompt: Which of these are learned weights (changed only by training), not per-request activations? Pick all that apply.

options.A: The output table used to score the next token
options.B: The attention weights (softmax shares) for this sentence
options.C: The embedding table
options.D: The query, key and value matrices (W_Q, W_K, W_V)
options.E: “bank”'s blended vector after attention in this sentence

prompt: “bank” is used in water sentences and in money sentences. Where does its embedding row end up?

options.A: Two separate rows, one per meaning, and the tokenizer picks which row each sentence uses
options.B: Somewhere between the water and money clusters; attention picks the meaning later from context
options.C: At a random spot, because the corrections from its two uses cancel out, so the row never moves
options.D: In the water cluster, because the first meaning seen in training fixes the row for good

prompt: Remove all position information. What happens to “dog bites man” versus “man bites dog”?

options.A: Only the last word's meaning is lost, since position mainly marks where the sentence ends
options.B: The tokenizer sorts the words alphabetically, so both sentences become the same token sequence
options.C: Attention receives the same set of vectors either way, so it can't tell the two orders apart
options.D: Order survives, because each token's embedding row already records where it appears

prompt: Which of these tasks are hard for an LLM for the same reason as counting letters? Pick all that apply.

options.A: Translating a common sentence
options.B: Exact arithmetic on long numbers
options.C: Reversing a word letter by letter
options.D: Finding words that rhyme

prompt: Why do LLMs split text into subword pieces rather than single characters?

options.A: Characters can't represent scripts other than Latin, so non-English text would need a separate tokenizer
options.B: A character vocabulary would hold millions of entries, too large to store as an embedding table
options.C: Characters make sequences several times longer, and attention's work grows with the square of length
options.D: A model can't learn spelling from single characters, so it would misspell words it has never seen

prompt: Context grows from 8,000 to 32,000 tokens. By what factor does the number of attention scores grow?
Compare softmax([3, 1]) with softmax([2, 0]).

options.A: The first is flatter, because both of its scores are further from zero
options.B: Identical: both come out at about 88% / 12%
options.C: The first gives the top score a bigger share, because its scores are larger
options.D: They can't be compared without knowing the rest of the vocabulary

prompt: Compute the dot product of [2, 1, 0] and [1, 3, 5].
Softmax of the scores [2, 0]. What share does the first score get, in percent? (e ≈ 2.718)
In “The river bank flooded”, which words can “bank” attend to?

options.A: All four words, including “flooded”
options.B: Only “river”, the word right before it
options.C: “The” and “river”, but not itself
options.D: “The”, “river”, and “bank” itself

prompt: How does byte-pair encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary?

options.A: Learn the pieces by gradient descent while the model trains, so the splits improve with the model
options.B: Start from single bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent neighbouring pair into a new token
options.C: Linguists write a list of common prefixes, roots and suffixes, and every word is split along them
options.D: Split the text at spaces, keep the most common words, and spell out every rarer word letter by letter

prompt: Why must the attention shares add up to 100%?

options.A: So they can be read as the probabilities of the next token, which the model then samples from
options.B: So that negative scores cancel positive ones and the strongest match always gets exactly half the weight
options.C: The next step is a weighted average; shares summing to 1 keep the blend on the same scale as the inputs
options.D: GPUs require normalized numbers, so any vector entering a multiply must already sum to 1

prompt: A tokenizer has no single piece for four spaces. What happens when you send it Python code indented with four spaces?

options.A: The tokenizer drops runs of spaces it has no piece for, so the code reaches the model with broken indentation
options.B: Nothing changes: whitespace is stripped before billing, so indentation costs no tokens at all
options.C: Each indent becomes several tokens, so the same code costs more and fills the context window sooner
options.D: The tokenizer rejects text containing a sequence it has no single piece for, so the whole request fails

prompt: Why don't LLMs use whole words as tokens?

options.A: Whole words make sequences longer than subwords do, so attention's square-law cost would grow too fast
options.B: Whole words can't be turned into vectors, because an embedding row needs a fixed number of characters
options.C: Attention can only compare pieces shorter than a word, so a whole-word token would be invisible to it
options.D: The vocabulary would need millions of entries and still fail on unseen words: new names, typos, identifiers

prompt: Put one attention step for “bank” in the right order.

options.A: key · each query → softmax → divide by √(head size) → weighted average of the values
options.B: query · each value → divide by √(head size) → softmax → weighted average of the keys
options.C: softmax of the keys → dot with the query → divide by √(head size) → sum of the values
options.D: query · each key → divide by √(head size) → softmax → weighted average of the values

prompt: Why use three separate vectors (query, key, value) instead of the token's embedding for everything?

options.A: One vector is needed per attention head, and the standard design happens to use three heads
options.B: To store three times as many facts per token, since each of the three vectors holds a different set of facts
options.C: Looking, matching and handing over are different jobs; separate learned matrices let each be tuned on its own
options.D: Embeddings can't be multiplied with each other directly, so each is first copied into three forms that can

prompt: Which backend operation has the same cost shape as attention over n tokens?

options.A: A single sequential scan over the rows: n, doubling as n doubles
options.B: A self-join comparing every row with every earlier row: about n²/2
options.C: A B-tree index lookup per row: log n each, so about n log n in total
options.D: A hash lookup per row: constant time each, so the total work is n

prompt: The score for “flooded” is bank's row · flooded's output row. After one training step, one column of bank's row moved a lot and another didn't move at all. Why?

options.A: The column that didn't move had already reached its best value in earlier training, so its gradient was zero
options.B: Training picks a few columns at random each step and updates only those, which keeps every step cheap enough
options.C: Each column's nudge is proportional to the matching column in flooded's row; a near-zero column gets no nudge
options.D: Only columns with large values get trained; small columns are frozen to keep the row stable

prompt: A model learns positions as a second table with one row per slot (slots 1 to 4,096). What does that design imply?

options.A: A hard length limit: input past slot 4,096 has no row to read
options.B: The vocabulary must also have 4,096 tokens
options.C: Word order stops mattering, since a table can't express which slot comes first
options.D: Positions keep being relearned at inference, so each request adjusts the slot table

prompt: Every token scores itself and every earlier token: n(n+1)/2 scores. How many scores for 4,000 tokens (per head, per layer)?
A model is 4,096 numbers wide and runs 32 attention heads. How many numbers wide is each head?
A language needs 3× as many tokens for the same meaning. What follows? Pick all that apply.

options.A: Less text fits in the context window
options.B: The model has more weights for that language
options.C: Higher cost per request (billed per token)
options.D: Prefill gets faster

prompt: Nobody labels “river” and “stream” as related. How do their embedding rows end up close?

options.A: Attention copies one row into the other at inference time whenever both words appear in one request
options.B: A synonym dictionary is loaded before training, and each listed pair of rows starts out close together
options.C: They fill the same slots in sentences (“the ___ overflowed”), so training nudges their rows the same way
options.D: The tokenizer gives similar words neighbouring IDs, and neighbouring IDs are given neighbouring rows
